claims.statement: Thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin, brand name Zadaxin) has no FDA-approved drug label in the United States - DailyMed, the authoritative U.S. label repository, returns zero results for "thymalfasin" - and is available in the U.S. only through compounding, not as an approved product; it is approved as a marketed drug in dozens of other countries (commonly cited for hepatitis B/C and as a cancer/vaccine adjuvant), but that ex-U.S. approval status has not been independently verified here against a primary foreign regulator source.

context.route: subcutaneous injection (product form used in approved markets and compounding)

claims.statement: FDA's evaluation of thymosin alpha-1 (Tα1, free base and acetate) for the 503A compounding Bulks List found that a balancing of the four evaluation criteria weighs against adding it, citing insufficient physicochemical characterization, an immunogenicity risk potentially amplified by aggregation and peptide-related impurities, and a proposed injectable concentration (3 mg/mL) that exceeds Ta1 free base's aqueous solubility (2 mg/mL); the nomination was subsequently withdrawn and FDA is evaluating the substance at its own discretion rather than under a completed rulemaking.

context.formulation: Tα1 free base and Tα1 acetate
context.useCase: regulatory evaluation for compounding eligibility (503A Bulks List)

The proposed concentration for injectable product (3 mg/mL) is greater than the solubility of Tα1 (free base) in water (2 mg/mL).
The nomination was withdrawn, and FDA is evaluating the substances at its discretion.

reviewFlags: nomination was withdrawn rather than formally decided - status is not a final FDA determination and must be re-checked against the live FDA compounding bulk substances list at review time

claims.statement: FDA's bulk drug substance evaluation flags a potential safety concern specific to immunosuppressed patients: thymosin alpha-1's immune-stimulating activity could cause or worsen acute or chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) and lead to engraftment failure in hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) recipients.

context.population: patients undergoing deliberate immunosuppression, including HSCT recipients
context.useCase: safety warning for immunocompromised or transplant populations

claims.statement: Thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) is a synthetically manufactured 28-amino-acid acetylated polypeptide identical to a naturally occurring human thymic peptide; it is described as activating toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) signaling on dendritic cells, driving Th1 polarization and T-cell maturation as part of coordinated adaptive immune responses.

extractedEvidence.quote: Thymalfasin is a chemically synthesized version of thymosin alpha 1 that is identical to human thymosin alpha 1.
Thymosin alpha 1 is an acetylated polypeptide.
Activates toll-like receptor 9 signaling on dendritic cells, driving Th1 polarization, T-cell maturation, and coordinated adaptive immune responses.

reviewFlags: mechanism sourced partly from a vendor-education page rather than a peer-reviewed pharmacology review; corroborate against a primary pharmacology reference at review time

claims.statement: In the largest and most rigorous published human efficacy trial - TESTS, a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in 1,106 adults with sepsis across 22 Chinese centers - subcutaneous thymosin alpha-1 every 12 hours for up to 7 days did not reduce 28-day all-cause mortality versus placebo (23.4% vs 24.1%; hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.77-1.27, p=0.93), and secondary/safety outcomes showed no significant differences between groups.

context.population: adults (18-85) with sepsis per Sepsis-3 criteria (n=1,106 randomized, 1,089 analyzed)
context.doseText: subcutaneous injection every 12 hours for up to 7 days or until ICU discharge/death/consent withdrawal (trial protocol; not a use recommendation)

extractedEvidence.quote: This trial found no clear evidence to suggest that thymosin α1 decreases 28 day all cause mortality in adults with sepsis.

reviewFlags: trial dose/protocol context must never be presented as a use recommendation
this is the highest-powered human RCT identified for any thymosin alpha-1 indication in this packet and should anchor efficacy framing over smaller/older positive trials

claims.statement: An earlier, smaller multicenter randomized controlled trial (ETASS, six Chinese hospitals, n=361 ICU patients with severe sepsis, 2008-2010) reported a numerically lower 28-day death rate with thymosin alpha-1 added to conventional therapy versus conventional therapy alone (26.0% vs 35.0%; relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.54-1.02), a difference that did not reach conventional statistical significance, alongside greater improvement in monocyte HLA-DR expression (an immune-function marker) in the treatment group.

context.useCase: severe sepsis (investigational; not an approved indication)

reviewFlags: superseded in statistical power and rigor by the later, larger TESTS phase 3 trial, which found no mortality benefit - see conflict entry

claims.statement: Thymosin alpha-1 is marketed and discussed online as having been "long recognized for modifying, enhancing, and restoring immune function," with popular interest extending to autoimmune disease management, general inflammation reduction, cancer support, and longevity-adjacent uses such as long COVID; the only large, rigorous, placebo-controlled human trial identified for a systemic-immunomodulation indication (sepsis) found no mortality benefit, and consumer-facing sources themselves acknowledge that findings for these broader immune/longevity uses are based on small trials and that "more research is needed." No controlled human evidence for general immune optimization, anti-aging, or wellness use in healthy adults was identified in this review.

conflicts.summary: The smaller, earlier ETASS trial (n=361, single-blind) reported a non-significant trend toward lower mortality with thymosin alpha-1 in severe sepsis, while the later, much larger TESTS phase 3 trial (n=1,106, double-blind, placebo-controlled) found no mortality benefit at all (HR 0.99, p=0.93). The discordance has not been independently adjudicated here against a third source family (e.g., a post-TESTS systematic review/meta-analysis specifically weighting trial quality); a 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis on this topic was identified in search results but not yet fetched and read for this packet.

A slide presentation submitted to an FDA public docket (regulations.gov, FDA-2024-N-4777-0009 attachment 7) asserts thymosin alpha-1/Zadaxin was "FDA approved to treat Hepatitis B," which directly conflicts with DailyMed showing zero approved labels for thymalfasin and a secondary source stating Zadaxin "has never been submitted for or granted FDA approval." This packet treats the DailyMed absence-of-label finding as controlling, but the source of the conflicting claim (a public commenter's presentation, not FDA itself) was not independently re-verified against a primary orphan-drug-designation or historical NDA record in this session.
